provenance: Factory baseline. The driver lower bounds come from the vendor's official release notes (checked 2026-08-08); every other rule came out of a real run, with its source in the entry's own note.

cu124.note: Measured basis, same as cu128: driver 535.154.05 ran a cu128 wheel with a real matmul on the card, so the vendor family minimum for self-contained runtimes (12.x ≥525.60) is the right number for the wheel path; the figure that used to be here came from the CUDA **toolkit** table, a different scenario. An older CUDA cannot need a newer driver than a newer CUDA does. Evidence: a probe run on rented hardware, its pass/fail criteria written down before it started.

cu126.note: Measured basis, same as cu128: driver 535.154.05 ran a cu128 wheel with a real matmul on the card, so the vendor family minimum for self-contained runtimes (12.x ≥525.60) is the right number for the wheel path; the figure that used to be here came from the CUDA **toolkit** table, a different scenario. An older CUDA cannot need a newer driver than a newer CUDA does. Evidence: a probe run on rented hardware, its pass/fail criteria written down before it started.

cu128.note: Measured 2026-08-10 on a rented RTX A4000 with driver **535.154.05**: pip-installed cu128 torch 2.11.0 reported CUDA 12.8, torch.cuda.is_available() was true, and a real matmul ran on the card and matched the CPU result (not just the self-report). So the vendor's family minimum for **applications that carry their own CUDA runtime** -- 11.x ≥450, 12.x ≥525, 13.x ≥580 -- holds for the path we actually take, and it is the number to use here. The earlier 570.26 (and then 550.54) came from the vendor's minimum-driver table for the **CUDA toolkit**, which is a different scenario; 535 is the most common long-term-support driver on rented GPUs, so that mistake blocked most machines. Evidence: a probe run on rented hardware, its pass/fail criteria written down before it started. PTX-JIT on a card newer than the wheel is a real exception, and it is checked separately by check_gpu_arch -- this row only answers the CUDA-family question.

cu130.note: CUDA 13.x needs driver ≥580 on Linux. **Checked 2026-08-10 and kept deliberately**: this one happens to match the vendor's toolkit table because the family minimum for self-contained runtimes is also 580 for 13.x -- so unlike the 12.x rows it was never wrong. Source: the vendor's driver-compatibility notes; no measurement of our own yet, which is why it is not lowered.

required_cpu_flags.note: Measured on a real run: the restore was byte-for-byte identical, yet importing a numerical library raised an illegal-instruction fault -- the host CPU was older and lacked the instruction set the wheel was built for.

egress.note: Measured on a real run: a machine being alive is not the same as a machine being usable -- egress to the code host was slow enough that cloning timed out. Threshold matched to the harness's fast-failure limit.

cuda_family_consistency.note: Measured on a real run: PyTorch was pinned to a CUDA 12.4 build, while an editable install with extras resolved a companion audio package to a CUDA 13 build from the default index -- two CUDA lines in one environment, ending in a missing runtime library. Pinning PyTorch alone is not enough; every CUDA-bound package in the family has to stay on the same line.

lock_cuda_vs_driver.note: Measured on a real run: following the framework's own README installed a PyTorch build for CUDA 13, while the host driver only supported CUDA 12.4. What the user sees is "your setup doesn't support bf16/gpu", which reads as "my graphics card is too old" -- when the real cause is a PyTorch build too new for the driver, and has nothing to do with the card. This happened on the officially documented installation path, not on an improvised one.
